question: A 30-year-old woman develops fever, urticaria, arthralgia, and lymphadenopathy 10 days after receiving equine anti-snake venom serum. Her serum C3 and C4 levels are low and urinalysis shows proteinuria. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is responsible?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This is classic serum sickness — a Type III hypersensitivity reaction. At 7–14 days, the immune response to foreign equine proteins peaks; antigen–antibody complexes form in antigen excess, deposit in blood vessel walls, glomeruli, and joint synovium, and activate complement. Low C3 and C4 confirm complement consumption by deposited complexes. Proteinuria reflects glomerular immune complex deposition.

Incorrect. Type I reactions occur within seconds to minutes of re-exposure and are mediated by IgE-driven mast cell degranulation (anaphylaxis, urticaria alone). The 10-day latency, low complement levels, joint involvement, and renal involvement here indicate immune complex deposition (Type III), not IgE-mediated degranulation.

Incorrect. Type II reactions involve IgG or IgM directed against cell-surface or tissue-fixed antigens, causing cell destruction (e.g., haemolytic transfusion reaction, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia). Serum sickness involves circulating antigen–antibody complexes depositing in tissues (Type III), not antibodies targeting fixed cell-surface antigens.

Incorrect. Type IV reactions are T-cell mediated (e.g., Mantoux test at 48–72 hours, contact dermatitis). Serum sickness at 10 days with systemic features, complement consumption (low C3/C4), and proteinuria from glomerular immune complex deposition is Type III hypersensitivity — antibody-mediated, not T-cell mediated.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the Gell and Coombs classification: Type I (IgE, seconds–minutes), Type II (cytotoxic IgG/IgM, cell-surface targets), Type III (immune complexes, 7–14 days, complement consumption), Type IV (T-cell, 48–72 hours).

Excellent! You correctly identified serum sickness as Type III hypersensitivity — remember the triad of 7–14 day latency, complement consumption, and immune complex deposition in vessels, glomeruli, and joints.
